THE
synthesis of methanol consists in directly com-
bining carbon monoxide with hydrogen at high pres-
sure in accordance with the equation

This reaction liberates about 843 gram-calories per gram of
alcohol produced and transforms into the liquid form 82.7
per cent of the heat content of the reacting gases, the re-
maining 17.3 per cent being dissipated in the form of heat.
In a gas mixture having the theoretical composition of carbon
monoxide and hydrogen in the ratio 1:2, the percentage, x, of
the carbon monoxide converted into methanol at equilibrium
is defined approximately by Nernst’s formula,

The values of x and y as calculated from equations (2) and (3)

that only relatively low pressures are required to effect the

In the synthesis of methanol, as in any other reaction be-
tween gases in contact with a solid catalyst, the rate of prod-
uct formation is of utmost importance from the point of
view of industrial feasibility.
This rate is best expressed as
the amount of alcohol wdiich can
be obtained per unit time
per unit volume of catalyst, and is a function of the following
variables: (1) the nature of the catalyst used, (2) the chem-
ical composition of the gas mixture at the point of intro-
duction to the catalyst mass, (3) the temperature of the gas
at that point, (4) the pressure of the gas, (5) the velocity
of the gas in the catalyst zone, and (6) the heat distribution
within the catalyst.
For
a given catalyst and
gas
com-
position the first two variables are fixed while the following

Obviously the heat distribution
within the catalyst mass depends both on the amount of heat
developed by the exothermic reaction in question and upon
the rate of dissipation of this heat.
While the heat developed varies with the activity of the
catalyst, the rate of heat removal depends only upon the ar-
rangement of the catalyst chamber.
The consequence is that
two experiments, made with the same
apparatus and under
the same conditions with two catalysts of different activities,
have different rates of heat transmission, and for that reason
are not strictly comparable with each other.
It is therefore
necessary, if the results obtained are to have any meaning,
to reduce to a minimum the effect of the variations in the
rate of heat transfer between the catalyst mass and the sur-
rounding medium for different experiments.
In order to
secure
operating conditions as nearly isothermal as possible,
the following three precautions were
resorted to, with the
result that the temperature difference between various points
in the catalyst bed was kept within 5° C.
First, the gas mixtures employed contained carbon monox-
ide and hydrogen in the ratio 1:5, rather than in the theo-
retical ratio 1:2, thereby utilizing the diluent effect of the excess
hydrogen to keep the temperature down.
^Second, the space
velocity was regulated so as to give a low value for the heat
liberated per second per cubic centimeter of catalyst.
Since
a pressure of 150 atmospheres was
consistently employed,
the adopted space velocity of 5000 corresponded to a time of
contact of 28 seconds at 250° C. and 23.5 seconds at 350° C.
Third, the apparatus was
constructed in a form which in-
sured the most rapid dissipation of heat from the catalyst
bed.
To accomplish this the catalyst was
placed in a thin-
walled tube of small diameter provided with a large number
of longitudinal flanges.
The catalyst tube, which had
a
capacity of only 15 cc., was then placed inside a high-pres-
sure chamber of about 2000 cc. volume, maintained at a gas
pressure
of
150
atmospheres.
By this arrangement the
catalyst tube was intimately in contact with a gas volume, the
specific heat of which was
about 45 gram-calories, or
more
than ten times the amount of heat set free per second in the
catalyst zone.
Apparatus

The high-pressure chamber, E, capable of withstanding the
working pressure,
is heated externally by
an
electric
re-
sistance wire.
The axial tube, T, is of small diameter with,
large contact surface, and holds the catalyst in position by

In Figure 4 is shown a set of reactors and in Figure 5 the

Preparation of Gas Mixtures
To avoid catalyst poisoning electrolytic hydrogen
was
used.
The carbon monoxide, which was prepared by dehy-
dration of formic acid with sulfuric acid, was treated with a
solution of sodium hydroxide in vertical tubes filled with
Raschig rings to
remove
vapors of formic acid and any
sulfur-containing
compounds
which
might
have
resulted
from reduction of the sulfuric acid.
Owing to the sensitivity of
methanol catalysts to poisoning by iron carbonyl, precautions
were taken to line all steel parts of the apparatus with some
other metal.
Furthermore, the gas mixtures were
always
carefully purified before entering the reaction chamber.
Method of Preparing Catalysts
From information
contained
in
Sabatier’s
treatise
on
“Catalysis in Organic Chemistry” as well as from the present
observations, it was
apparent that the highest activity was
obtained when the catalyst was prepared at low temperature.
The various oxides investigated were
therefore subjected to a
reducing atmosphere at comparatively low temperatures.
A slow current of hydrogen, at times charged with methanol
(methanol was used in the reduction of the oxides of molyb-
denum, vanadium, tungsten, titanium, and uranium),
was
passed over
the catalyst, the temperature being maintained
at 200° C. during the first 4 hours and at 300° C. during the
next 14 hours.
When the catalysts were
prepared by the
wet method, the hydroxides were
dried to constant weight
in an
oven
at 110° C. before reduction.
Since the time of contact between the gas and the catalyst
for a constant inlet rate of flow depends upon the porosity of
the contact mass, efforts were
made to prepare the different
catalysts in the form of grains of substantially the same shape
and dimensions.
To this end the hydroxides, etc., from
which the catalysts were
prepared, were
pressed in the form
of a paste through a die of 1.5 mm.
diameter.
The filaments
thus obtained were
dried and broken into fragments about
1.5 to 3 mm.
long.
CATALYST STUDIES
In
choosing catalysts for the synthesis of methanol it
was desirable to start by determining the properties of those
substances which Sabatier had found to be capable of de-
composing methanol at atmospheric pressure into carbon
monoxide and hydrogen.
These substan’ces
were
copper,
cobalt, iron, platinum, nickel, and palladium,
as well
as
certain metallic oxides.
The results obtained with these
and other catalysts are presented in the following:
Inert
Oxides
Not even the slightest trace of methanol was formed with
any of the following eleven oxides: alumina, silica, molyb-
denum oxide (M02O5), vanadium oxide
(V2O3), blue tung-
sten oxide (W205), thoria, titanium oxide (T1O2), magnesia,
lime, barium oxide, and strontium oxide.
Most of these
substances
as prepared—especially alumina, silica, thoria,
titanium
oxide,
magnesia,
and lime—had
a
composition
between that of the hydrates from which they were
derived
and that of the anhydrous oxides obtained by prolonged
calcination at higher temperature.
Active Oxides
Seven other oxides investigated were
more
or less active,
the efficiency—that is, per cent of the entering carbon mon-
oxide converted to
methanol at 150 atmos-
pheres and a space ve-
locity of 5000—of the
following four being
less than
2 per cent:
cerous
oxide
(Ce20s),
black uranium dioxide
(UO2), beryllium oxide
(BeO), and zirconium
oxide (ZrCb).
The
three other oxides stud-
ied were
manganous
oxide (877), chromium
sesquioxide (878), and
zinc oxide
(856), pre-
pared by precipitation
of the hydrates from the
corresponding nitrates
by
means
of sodium

for these three catalysts
are given in Table I.

The activities of the catalysts are not, however,
c

Thus, a brand

with that of chromium sesquioxide—i. e., much lower than
that of the zinc oxide listed in column
1 of Table I.
This
low activity persisted even
after the zinc oxide had been
dissolved in pure nitric
acid, reprecipitated with sodium
hydroxide, dehydrated, and reduced by the regular method.
Metallic
Copper
As has already been pointed out by Sabatier, the properties
of copper catalysts are profoundly influenced by the method
of preparation.
In general, active copper can
be prepared
only by reduction of the oxide, and it is essential that the
temperature of reduction be kept at a minimum, since under
otherwise constant conditions the activity of the resulting
copper varies inversely with the temperature developed during
reduction.
Hence, in preparing the various copper catalysts
described below, care
was taken to prevent the temperature
from rising above 250® C.
The results show some
rather
remarkable relationships between the methods of preparation
and the activities of the resulting catalysts.
Hydrated Cupric Oxide—When a solution of alkali hy-
droxide is added to
a boiling solution of copper nitrate a
black precipitate is formed, commonly
called “tetra cupric hydrate” and corre-
sponding to the formula 4Cu0.H60,
By
reduction of the. precipitate with hydro-
gen, Sabatier obtained a copper of low
density and purplish color, characterized
by high catalytic activity, and capable of
decomposing methanol into carbon mon-
oxide and hydrogen at atmospheric pres-
sure.
When the alkali-precipitated hy-
drate is heated above 300° C., it under-
goes a transformation accompanied by a
change in color and density.
If, however,
the temperature is kept below 300° C.,
the tetra cupric hydrate loses water gradu-
ally and is finally converted to anhydrous
cupric oxide without any change what-
ever in appearance, apparent density, or
temperature at which it starts to reduce.
These observations did not leave much
evidence in favor of the assumption of a
definite compound, and it was deemed de-
sirable to
compare the activity of the
catalysts produced un-
der varying conditions
of dehydration.
A
portion of the alkali-
precipitated cupric hy-
drate, washed with dis-
tilled water until
neu-
tral to phenolphthalein,
was
therefore divided
into four portions and
heated to various tem-
peratures for a period
of 3 to 4 hours prior to
reduction.
The data
for these catalysts,
given in Table II and
Figure 6, show some
variation
in the per-
centage of carbon mon-
oxide converted
to
methanol.
Since the
,
catalyst volume was

the variation in weight
must be taken into con-
sideration.
Thus, it is
apparent that the con-
versions realized with
catalysts 713 and 717
are
roughly
propor-
tional to their weights.
However, the fact
that the efficiencies of
the two other catalysts,
715 and 716, are about
30 per cent higher than

basis, points to
the

low-temperature dehy-

of the cupric
hydrate.

Its activity was perceptibly

Cupric Oxide from
Calcination
of
Organic Salts—As might be expected,
the oxides obtained by decomposition at
low temperature of the unstable organic
salts, such as the formate and acetate,
give catalysts of approximately the same
activity as those prepared by reduction
of tetra cupric hydrate.

may be considered an intermediate step
in the reduction of cupric oxide, was pre-
pared by treatment of freshly reduced cop-
per with nitrogen peroxide at 210-220° C.
(Sabatier).
The reduction of this com-
pound with hydrogen resulted in a cata-

Recalculated on
a weight basis,
however, the conversion falls in between

obtained by reduc-

This is probably due to the
poisoning effect of the adsorbed anion.
Cupric Oxide Precipitated
from
Nitrate
Solution in
the
Cold—In
concluding the investigation of copper,
a
study was
made of the properties of catalysts prepared from
oxide precipitated with ammonia from a cold nitrate solution.
The fact that this metal was completely inactive pointed to
a promoter action of traces of alkali adsorbed on the tetra
cupric hydrate catalysts described above.
However,
ex-
tensive experiments involving various
degrees of washing

Summary op Studies on Copper—It is apparent that cu-
prous and cupric oxides give active catalysts by reduction
with hydrogen.
The method of preparing the
oxides
is
important, however, and it is essential that the reduction be
carried out at low temperature.
Metals Other than Copper
The metals iron, cobalt, nickel, platinum, and palladium,
which all decompose methanol at atmospheric pressure, may
a priori be expected to catalyze the reverse reaction—i. e., the
high-pressure synthesis of methanol.
However, these metals
are also catalysts for the reactions
2CO
=
C + C02 + 42,000 calories
(4)
CO + 3H2
=
CH4 + H20 + 51,100 calories
(5)
2CO + 2H2
=
CH4 + C02 + 61,000 calories
(6)
which all go with a decrease in volume, and hence methanol
production is always accompanied by the formation of varying
amounts of elementary carbon, carbon dioxide, and methane.
Thus, the percentage of carbon monoxide converted to meth-
anol by nickel is practically negligible compared with that
entering into the above side reactions.
This result is not
surprising in view of the fact that the equilibrium conditions
are considerably more
favorable to methane production than
to the formation of methanol.
By the application of Nernst’s theorem and the equilibrium
data of Hahn2 for the reaction
CO + H20
=
C02 + H2 + 9900 calories
(7)
it may be shown that methane and water predominate at
equilibrium at the pressure here employed (150 atmospheres)
as long
as the temperature does not
exceed 700° C.
In
other words, reaction
(5)
is favored thermodynamically,
leaving practically no
room
for carbon dioxide at equilibrium
under the conditions of the experiment.
Nevertheless, it
was
found that carbon dioxide resulted when reduced (or
perhaps only partly reduced) iron was
used as the catalyst
at
150 atmospheres and temperatures below 700° C. with
a gas mixture containing carbon monoxide and hydrogen in
the ratio 1:5.
Undoubtedly, therefore, reaction (6) must

It is impossible to say, however, whether
the water vapor simultaneously formed resulted from
re-
action (5), or whether it was produced by interaction of the
initially formed carbon dioxide with hydrogen by reversal
of reaction (7).
Effect of Heat
on Activity of Methanol
Catalysts
From
a commercial point of view the sensitivity of
a
catalyst to heat is a most important factor.
It is well known
that such metals as nickel, iron, cobalt, platinum, palladium,
and copper lose their activity
as hydrogenation catalysts
when subjected to prolonged heating at sufficiently high
temperature,3 and hence it was deemed desirable to study the
effect of temperature on the activity of the methanol cata-
lysts discussed above.
In general, the decrease in activity of copper catalysts is
very pronounced when they are heated above the operating
temperature.
This loss in activity is most marked at the
beginning of the heat treatment, the effect of prolonged heat-
ing being progressively less.
Thus, preheating a copper cata-
lyst promoted with cerium oxide to 450° C. for 1 hour in an
atmosphere of hydrogen reduced the rate of methanol pro-
duction by about 45 per cent, while the corresponding drop
resulting from 22 hours’ heating was about 60 per cent.
Identical heat treatment of the copper catalysts in Table
II and Figure 6 demonstrated that the sensitivity to heat is
influenced by the method of preparation of the catalysts,
although it is impossible to lay down any simple rule for this
relation.
Furthermore, the higher the temperature to which
the catalyst is raised, the greater the loss in activity, as would
be expected.
Zinc oxide shows the some general behavior as copper, ex-
cept that it is somewhat more
sensitive to heat.
This may
be seen from the comparable data for zinc oxide and reduced
copper in Table III.

That this is actually

In these two
runs

were

The

Catalytic Properties of Mixtures
Numerous examples are
known of reactions whose rates
are enormously increased by catalysts composed of mixtures of
which one or more components are active when used alone.
In
studying the effect of such mixtures on the methanol reaction,
reduced copper was chosen as the basic constituent, since the
previous experiments had shown it to be the most active single
catalyst.
In
the systematic investigation
made,
a
large
variety of substances
were
added to copper and activity
tests made for each mixture.
While it may be objected that
this is an empirical method of attack and that one is liable
to leave unexplored some
particular mixture of outstanding
activity, it is nevertheless the only means of pursuing a search
for catalysts for a specific reaction.
Only by the assembling
of accurate and extended experimental data is it possible to
accumulate results for inspiration of fertile hypotheses.
A few of the results obtained in the course
of this work are
presented below.
All catalysts
were
prepared by precipi-
tation of the hydroxides from the mixed nitrate solutions
with a boiling solution of sodium hydroxide.
As before, a
gas mixture containing carbon monoxide and hydrogen in
the ratio 1:5 was used at a pressure of 150 atmospheres and
a space velocity of 5000.
For all mixtures the sensitivity to
heat was
determined by preheating separate samples of the
reduced catalyst to 450° C. for 6 hours in an atmosphere of
hydrogen.
Copper
and
Zinc
Oxide—The
results obtained with
mixtures of copper and zinc oxide are given in Table IV.
It
is apparent that the initial activity of copper is markedly in-
creased by the addition of relatively small amounts of zinc
oxide, but the catalyst mixtures are still sensitive to heat, as
is most clearly brought out by the corresponding curves
in
Figures 8 and 9.
Copper and
Manganous Oxide—The data in Table V
show a rapid increase in activity for small additions of man-
ganous oxide with a maximum at
a  -Cu
ratio approxi-
mating 3:100.
Further amounts of manganous oxide de-
crease
the activity, which reaches a minimum at a ratio of
about
15:100, followed by
a gradual increase to
a value
somewhat lower than the original maximum.
It
is also
interesting to note that the catalyst possessing maximum
activity is most sensitive to heat, while subsequent additions
of manganous oxide make it considerably more resistant.
Copper, Manganous Oxide,
and
Chromium Sesqui-
oxide—The results obtained with copper and manganous
oxide suggested the addition of
a third compound to the
two mixtures which possessed the maximum ac-
tivity without and with preheating—viz., Mn-Cu
=
3:100 and 37.5:100.
Chromium sesquioxide
was
chosen for this purpose.
From Figure 10 it will be seen that the addition
of chromium sesquioxide to the mixture low in
manganous oxide yields catalysts of high
ac-
tivity and considerable resistance to heat.
The
mixtures of high manganous oxide content have
even
higher initial activity and are also rendered
less sensitive to heat by increasing amounts of
chromium sesquioxide.
Copper, Manganous Oxide, and Beryllium
Oxide—The substitution of beryllium for chro-
mium in the preceding mixtures gave less active
catalysts, showing that chromium sesquioxide is
preferable.
Copper
and
Alumina—Mixtures of copper
and alumina give irregular activity curves
with
several maxima and minima.
The highest effi-
ciency is obtained with an Al-Cu ratio of 15:100,
corresponding to 90 per cent conversion of the
entering carbon monoxide.
The resistance to heat is also
variable and not very high, the two activity curves
being of
the same general form (Figures 8 and 9).
Copper and Zirconium Oxide—The addition of zirconium
oxide to copper fails to bring the conversion above 67 per cent,
a value which must be considered low compared with some
of the other mixtures investigated.

Summary and Conclusions
From the results presented in this paper it is apparent that a
number of substances which decompose methanol at elevated
temperature and atmospheric pressure are capable of catalyz-
ing the synthesis of the alcohol by the reverse
reaction using
carbon monoxide and hydrogen at high pressure.
Reduced copper and zinc oxide are the most active of the
methanol catalysts
studied.
Manganous oxide and chro-
mium sesquioxide are of a considerably lower order, and the
remaining oxides are too inactive to consider it worth while
to employ them alone.
The method of preparing the catalysts is of utmost impor-
tance.
This has been brought out particularly by the exten-
sive studies of copper, showing that cuprous and cupric oxides
give active catalysts with reduction by hydrogen, when pre-
pared by precipitation of the nitrate or by thermal decomposi-
tion of the unstable copper salts of organic acids.
It is essen-
tial that the reduction be carried out at low temperature.
Copper catalysts prepared from the hydroxide precipitated
from solutions of the sulfate and chloride are entirely in-
active.
All of these single-component catalysts are very sensitive to
heat, as has been brought out by the lowering in methanol
conversion resulting from heat treatment somewhat above the
temperature of operation.
In general, mixed catalysts are superior to single-component
catalysts, as manifested both by the great increase in the rate
of methanol production and by the greater resistance to heat.
In regard to the behavior of mixed catalysts, the material
here presented does not permit of any definite conclusions.
The data plotted for a large variety of such mixtures in
Figures 8 and 9 are too erratic for a simple interpretation.
